content: Kepone, also referred to as chlordecone, is a carcinogenic insecticide chemically related to mirex. It was utilized in the United States between 1966 and 1975, primarily as an ingredient in ant and roach baits. The substance was manufactured by the Allied Signal Company in Hopewell, Virginia. However, improper handling and disposal of Kepone, including its release into the James River, led to significant nationwide environmental pollution concerns. Its use was officially banned in 1975. From a chemical perspective, Kepone is classified as a chlorinated polycyclic ketone insecticide and fungicide, with the molecular formula C10H2Cl10O. The substance exists as a dry powder that can be readily absorbed through the skin and respiratory tract, posing significant health risks upon exposure. Workers who were unprotected during the production of Kepone experienced a range of severe health effects, including tremors, involuntary eye movements (nystagmus), memory impairment, headaches, slurred speech, unsteadiness, poor coordination, weight loss, skin rashes, hepatomegaly (enlarged liver), reduced libido, infertility, chest pain, joint pain (arthralgia), and an elevated risk of cancer development. Kepone is highly persistent in the environment, with an estimated half-life of approximately 30 years. The environmental and health impacts of Kepone were brought to national attention in part due to investigative reporting by Dan Rather and CBS's 60 Minutes. A 2005 article in Richmond Magazine detailed the adverse health effects experienced by Allied Signal employees and highlighted the broader consequences of the Kepone crisis. The pollution scare caused by Kepone had significant economic repercussions. Numerous businesses and restaurants along the James River suffered losses, and then-Governor Mills Godwin Jr. ordered the closure of the James River to fishing activities from Richmond to the Chesapeake Bay. In a cultural context, the Kepone crisis inspired a song written in 1978, which was performed live but not officially recorded until 1981. Additionally, the crisis influenced the naming of an American indie rock band, Kepone, which was formed in Richmond, Virginia, in 1991. The band’s name directly references the environmental disaster that occurred in the Richmond area during the 1970s. The band was initially created as a side project by Michael Bishop, the former bassist of the band GWAR.
